title: SDSS-V Maps the Galaxy With New All-Sky Spectra, Including Southern Hemisphere Firsts - Bioengineer.org
content: The Sloan Digital Sky Survey V has released its twentieth public data release, opening access to more than two million stellar spectra and offering astronomers the most extensive spectroscopic view yet of the Milky Way and its surrounding regions. Known as DR20, the release significantly expands the survey’s Milky Way Mapper program, which is designed to chart stars across the Galaxy by measuring their temperatures, ages, motions, and chemical compositions. The observations were collected with twin optical spectrographs at Apache Point Observatory in New Mexico and Las Campanas Observatory in Chile, providing a combined view of the northern and southern skies. Unlike a conventional photograph, a stellar spectrum records how a star emits or absorbs light at different wavelengths. These patterns reveal the elements present in a star’s atmosphere, its surface temperature, and, when combined with other observations, clues about its age and movement. Because stars retain chemical information from the environments in which they formed, millions of spectra can be used to reconstruct the Milky Way’s history. Repeated observations also allow researchers to identify changes in brightness and motion, making the data useful for studying stellar systems, binary stars, and energetic objects. One of DR20’s major scientific advances is the public release of the first large dataset from the Milky Way Mapper Halo Program. The program focuses on the faint, diffuse halo surrounding the Galaxy’s bright disk. This region contains some of the oldest stars known and preserves evidence of smaller galaxies that were absorbed by the Milky Way over billions of years. The newly released sample includes spectra for approximately 250,000 halo stars, including distant giant stars observed across the sky, rapidly moving stars close to the Sun, and extremely metal-poor stars whose atmospheres contain less than one percent of the iron found in the Sun. Metal-poor stars are especially valuable to galactic archaeologists because they formed when the Universe contained relatively few elements heavier than hydrogen and helium. Their chemical compositions preserve conditions that existed shortly after the first generations of stars began enriching cosmic space. Their orbits provide another layer of evidence: unusual trajectories can reveal the remnants of ancient satellite galaxies or gravitational encounters that shaped the Milky Way. By combining spectroscopy with stellar distances and motions, researchers can trace structures in the halo that are almost invisible in ordinary images. The release also more than doubles the number of publicly available white dwarf spectra from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, adding about 49,000 observations. White dwarfs are the compact remnants left behind when stars similar in mass to the Sun exhaust their nuclear fuel and shed their outer layers. Their interiors are supported by electron degeneracy pressure rather than ongoing nuclear fusion, and they gradually cool over billions of years. More than 80 percent of the white dwarfs in this new sample had not previously been observed by SDSS, while over 40 percent are located in the southern sky. Their atmospheres can contain traces of heavier elements, sometimes indicating that asteroids or planets were torn apart and accreted by the dead star. Closer to Earth, the Solar Neighborhood Census is assembling a detailed spectroscopic inventory of objects within 250 parsecs, or roughly 815 light-years, of the Sun. DR20 includes spectra for about 280,000 nearby stars, with particular attention to low-mass M dwarfs and brown dwarfs. These faint objects account for most of the stars in the Galaxy but are difficult to study because they emit relatively little visible light. By combining SDSS-V spectroscopy with precise distance measurements from the European Space Agency’s Gaia mission, astronomers can compare the masses, ages, chemical compositions, and motions of nearby stellar populations with unprecedented consistency. The data release also expands the Young Galaxy Program to more than 200,000 young stars and planetary nurseries, quadrupling its size compared with the previous release. Young stars often retain disks of gas and dust from which planets may form, while intense magnetic activity can produce powerful flares and high-energy radiation. The program also tracks massive O- and B-type stars, which live only a few million years but illuminate and shape their surroundings. Because these stars form preferentially along spiral arms, their distribution helps astronomers investigate how star formation moves through the Milky Way. Another component of DR20 links optical spectroscopy with observations from the European Space Agency’s eROSITA X-ray telescope. SDSS-V has obtained nearly 48,000 optical spectra of objects first identified as energetic X-ray sources. The combined dataset includes accreting binary systems, magnetic stars, and other sources capable of producing intense high-energy emission. X-rays often reveal processes hidden at visible wavelengths, such as material falling onto a compact stellar remnant or magnetic fields accelerating particles. Matching X-ray detections with optical spectra allows researchers to identify the objects responsible and determine their physical properties. The release is already being used to investigate ancient stars outside the Milky Way. A study led by Maddie Lucey reports the first five carbon-enhanced metal-poor stars identified in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Carbon-enhanced metal-poor stars are rare relics whose unusual abundances may reflect pollution by early supernovae or mass transfer from an evolved companion. Their discovery in the Large Magellanic Cloud gives astronomers a new way to test whether the oldest stars formed under different conditions in smaller galaxies. Related work using SDSS-V data has also examined the distant and metal-poor halo and reported an exceptionally pristine star associated with the Large Magellanic Cloud. By placing millions of measurements into public hands, SDSS-V is transforming the Milky Way from a collection of individual observations into a dynamic, chemically structured system that can be analyzed statistically. Researchers can use the spectra to identify stellar families, reconstruct merger events, measure the history of star formation, and examine how planetary systems survive the deaths of their host stars. The scale of DR20 also creates opportunities for discoveries that were not part of the survey’s original goals, as automated searches and independent studies examine the catalog for rare stars, unusual binaries, and previously overlooked phenomena. title: Gender identity and the Sex Discrimination Act: lessons from Giggle v Tickle - Law Society Journal
content: This litigation saga began when Roxanne Tickle, a transgender woman, commenced proceedings in the Federal Court against Giggle for Girls Pty Ltd (‘Giggle’) and its CEO, Sally Grover, after Tickle was removed from the Giggle for Girls App (‘App’) which was promoted as being a space for women only. In order to use the App, users had to upload a selfie which was then verified by AI gender-detection software. Roxanne Tickle did this, her photo was approved and she started using the App. However, seven months later, Grover removed Tickle from the platform after reviewing the selfie and deciding Tickle was not a woman. Tickle alleged discrimination on the basis of her gender identity under section 5B of the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) (‘SDA’). At first instance, the judge held Tickle had been indirectly discriminated against on the basis she did not look sufficiently female. That is, she was not judged by Grover to be a cisgender woman. His Honour awarded her $10,000 in damages and costs. Giggle and Grover appealed the decision and Tickle cross-appealed. The Full Federal Court dismissed the appeal and allowed the cross appeal, finding there had been direct discrimination, rather than indirect, and increasing the damages to $20,000, including $8,000 in aggravated damages. title: V Torres Leans Into Possibility On New Single “That Night” - That Eric Alper
content: V Torres captures the split second when friendship begins turning into something more on “That Night,” the newest preview of her forthcoming sophomore album, ‘Woman.’ Listen here. The Los Angeles-based singer-songwriter builds the song around the uncertainty of opening yourself up to someone and wondering what might happen if you cross that familiar line. “It’s highlighting that scary and exciting part of letting your guard down,” Torres says. Shimmering guitars and sweeping melodies give “That Night” a cinematic pull, while Torres keeps the emotional focus on possibility rather than resolution. The single follows “Woman” and “Winter Solstice,” 2 songs that have already introduced different sides of the upcoming 7-track record. ‘Woman’ moves through identity, resilience, grief, healing and self-discovery, with Torres co-producing the album alongside longtime collaborator Steve Aguilar. It’s also the first full-length record she has co-produced herself. Sonically, Torres stretches across indie rock, Americana, desert psychedelia and Latin influences, giving the album plenty of room to move while keeping her songwriting at the centre. The record was written during a period of significant change in Torres’ life, with its songs tracing endings, beginnings, heartbreak, freedom and renewal. Her musical foundation reaches back to a childhood spent digging through her parents’ record collection, where Pink Floyd, Steely Dan, Hank Williams Jr., Joni Mitchell, Janis Joplin, Jimi Hendrix and Earth, Wind & Fire all entered the mix. Torres later began performing original songs at open mics before playing Los Angeles venues including The Roxy Theatre and The Viper Room with her first band, Gorgeous Got a Gun. Fans will get 2 chances to hear the new material live in Southern California, beginning August 8 at The Studio in Hermosa Beach. She’ll also perform September 9 at The Mint in Los Angeles, supporting blues guitarist and vocalist Sue Foley. “That Night” is available now. ‘Woman’ arrives independently on September 1, with vinyl pre-orders available now. Eric Alper is a 6-time nominee for Publicist of the Year during Canadian Music Week and has overseen the publicity campaigns for over 183 JUNO Award-nominated albums (and 16 in 2025), 45 Grammy-nominated albums, including 47 JUNO Award, 58 Canadian Folk Music Award, 126 Maple Blues Award-winning albums and is also truly honoured to work with some of the biggest and most important artists of our time.

title: NRSC v. FEC: New Opportunities for Republicans in 2026 and Beyond - Campaigns & Elections
content: What’s the view from the Republican side on how much the Supreme Court’s decision in NRSC v. FEC changes ahead of this year’s midterms? Campaigns & Elections Editor-in-Chief Max Greenwood sat down with three GOP campaign finance and fundraising experts to talk through the short and long-term implications. The conversation included Jessica Furst Johnson, a partner at Lex Politica and former general counsel for three national political committees; Bradley Crate, president and co-founder of Red Curve Solutions, which manages FEC compliance and treasury operations for committees across the country; and Mike Hahn, president of digital at Frontline Strategies and an alum of the 2016 and 2020 Trump for President campaigns. The focus was largely on the structural implications: How will state parties and committees adapt in an environment where they can become more central strategic partners to campaigns across the country? What advantages do super PACs retain even after the ruling? And how are independent expenditure units and joint fundraising committees impacted? Watch the full conversation above.For the Democratic perspective, listen to C&E’s conversation with Brian Derrick, co-founder and CEO of Democratic fundraising platform Oath; Rachel Jacobs, partner at Elias Law Group and general counsel to the DCCC; and Brian Svoboda, a partner at Ashurst Perkins Coie. Chief product officer Jorn Lambert framed it as a bet on a "multi-money world," where fiat currency, stablecoins and tokenized deposits all need to work together rather than compete for the same transaction. BVNK's technology lets people, businesses and machines hold, move and convert value across fiat and digital currencies, built inside a compliance and security framework banks already trust. Mastercard says combining that on-chain infrastructure with its own global network should help financial institutions, fintechs and enterprises scale stablecoin use cases in cross-border B2B payments, remittances, payouts, settlement and treasury flows, the areas Lambert singled out as already showing real-world demand. The deal lands on top of a business that was already growing faster in several places than its biggest rival, drawing immediate comparison to Visa (NYSE:V) as investors weigh which payment giant is best positioned for the future. Mastercard's cross-border volume climbed 12% last quarter, trailing slightly behind the 13% growth Visa posted, and Mastercard's value-added services arm, the fraud, data, and consulting tools sold on top of the network, grew 20%. Adjusted EPS jumped 23%, ahead of Visa's 11%. Layering stablecoin infrastructure onto that growth gives Mastercard another lever in the cross-border and B2B payments categories where it has already been gaining ground. While Mastercard's $1.8 billion acquisition of BVNK has publicly clarified the cost of its push into blockchain infrastructure, stablecoin settlement remains a smaller, less-tested revenue stream than Mastercard's core card business. The EPS growth headline also overstates the underlying trend: strip out a currency tailwind and the real gain was closer to 18%, just shy of the 10% Visa posted in constant dollars. Additionally, on the same day, August 3, Visa announced a definitive agreement to buy fraud detection firm BioCatch for $2.4 billion in cash, adding AI-driven behavioral biometrics directly onto its rails. Both networks moved on the same day: Mastercard closed its BVNK acquisition while Visa announced its own BioCatch deal, each staking a claim to a different piece of the next-generation payments stack, stablecoin settlement for one, AI fraud defense for the other. Hedge fund ownership of Mastercard rose from 150 to 157 funds last quarter, while Visa's fell from 184 to 181, a split that favors Mastercard's momentum. As of August 4, Mastercard trades at a forward P/E of 29.15 against Visa's 24.45, a premium that assumes Mastercard's faster growth continues. Short interest is lighter on Mastercard, at 1.04% of float versus 1.39% for Visa, showing less organized skepticism despite the richer multiple. The BVNK deal gives Mastercard a meaningful position in stablecoin infrastructure at a time when its cross-border and value-added services businesses are already growing strongly. Mastercard's recent earnings growth has outpaced Visa's, but the $1.8 billion acquisition still needs to demonstrate that stablecoin usage can translate into material revenue and attractive returns. Until then, BVNK strengthens Mastercard's long-term payments strategy more clearly than it changes the company's near-term financial outlook. title: Storylines | Royals v. Summit: The Battle for the Continental Divide Cup - Real Salt Lake
content: Utah Royals FC head to Colorado this Saturday, August 8, for a key road match against Denver Summit FC at Centennial Stadium. Fresh off a historic 5-1 victory over the Portland Thorns, the most goals scored in a single match for Utah, the Royals will look to carry that momentum into another crucial contest against a Denver side that sits three points outside the playoff line. This edition of storylines will focus on how the Royals can build on its historic scoring performance, and take a closer look at how competitive Denver Summit FC has been in its first NWSL season. This season, Head Coach Jimmy Coenraets has emphasized offensive pressing as a defining identity of the team. Leading the effort has been Kiana Palacios, whose relentless running, front press, and anticipation allow her teammates to recognize where the ball will likely fall after the team win back possession. The Mexican international has played a pivotal role in leading the Royals' high press, an approach that has been instrumental in several of the club's victories this season. Her relentless work rate, closing speed, and ability to pressure defenders have made it extremely difficult for opposing teams to build out from the back, frequently forcing turnovers in dangerous areas and setting the tone for the Royals' defensive intensity. A prime example of Palacios’ ability to read the game and forward pressure came in the first meeting between Denver and Utah at America First Field, where she anticipated the direction of a loose ball, positioned herself quickly, and turned a defensive moment into a scoring opportunity. Fellow forward Cloé Lacasse won the ball off a Summit defender, creating a chance for Palacios to pounce on the loose ball inside the penalty area. The Mexican striker clinically fired a left-footed finish into the roof of the net beyond the outstretched Denver goalkeeper, to score her first NWSL goal. Most recently in the 5-1 victory against Portland, Palacios’ anticipation aided her in scoring her third goal this season. Running in between the two Thorns center back before cleverly finishing the cross with a back heel finish that left the away team’s goalkeeper frozen in place. In the same match, Palacios displayed her relentless pressing as the Thorns were forced to resort to long balls to get past the collective Royals front press. The Royals have faced off against the Summit once since Denver entered the NWSL with Utah winning the first meeting. A 72nd minute penalty from Mina Tanaka proved to be the difference, lifting Utah Royals FC to a 2-1 victory and securing all three points at America First Field. Since returning from the NWSL break, Denver Summit FC is 1-3-2 (W-L-T), most recently falling 2-0 at home on Wednesday to the North Carolina Courage. In a back-and-forth contest, the Courage broke through early in the second half by converting a penalty before sealing the result with a transition goal late in the match. title: National Ben Gamla Jewish Charter School Foundation, Inc. v. Shellem - Becket — Religious Liberty for All
content: Families across Oklahoma need better educational options for their children. The National Ben Gamla Jewish Charter School Foundation wants to help meet this need by joining Oklahoma’s charter school program and offering families a rigorous, values-based education that integrates academic excellence with religious learning. But the Oklahoma Supreme Court’s ruling in St. Isidore v. Drummond bars faith-based schools from joining the charter program. Ben Gamla is challenging that exclusion in federal court to ensure that religious schools can serve Oklahoma families. Opening doors to educational opportunities in the Sooner State Since 2007, Peter Deutsch has built a network of Hebrew-language charter schools, known as the Ben Gamla Charter Schools, across the state of Florida. They have served over twenty thousand diverse students and offer an education focused on Hebrew language, culture, and history. Ben Gamla schools have an outstanding record of academic excellence and ethical instruction, while also maintaining open admissions and diverse hiring of individuals who support their mission. Drawing on that experience, Deutsch incorporated the National Ben Gamla Jewish Charter School Foundation in Oklahoma and applied for charter authorization in Oklahoma to start an online charter school open to students of all faiths. He wants to give Sooner families a high-quality option that pairs strong academics with religious learning and spiritual formation. Oklahoma’s charter school regulations are uniquely suited to such educational innovation and would allow Ben Gamla to provide an education tailored to the individual needs of many diverse students. Oklahoma Supreme Court excludes faith-based charter schools Unfortunately, in March 2026, the Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board denied Ben Gamla’s application. While members of the Charter School Board praised Ben Gamla’s model, they determined that under the Oklahoma Supreme Court’s ruling in St. Isidore v. Drummond, faith-based charter schools are not allowed to participate on equal footing with other private schools. That case went all the way to the Supreme Court of the United States, which split 4–4, leaving the constitutional questions unresolved. Oklahoma has continued to treat St. Isidore as a blanket prohibition on religious charter schools. Becket fights for Ben Gamla’s right to serve Oklahoma families This is yet another example of government officials attempting to exclude religious groups from publicly available education benefits. In fact, Attorney General Drummond was honored as “Secularist of the Week” by anti-religion group Freedom From Religion Foundation for opposing Ben Gamla and other religious schools. Despite the Supreme Court’s clear guidance in Trinity Lutheran, Espinoza, and Carson—which held that religious institutions cannot be denied access to public funding simply because of their religious character—states continue to take steps that shut out religious schools from programs offered to other private institutions. title: The Honda SUV That Feels More Premium Than A Mercedes GLC - Top Speed
content: Few segments are as fiercely contested right now as the luxury SUV space, and yet some of the most compelling value propositions are coming from brands you might not expect. While Porsche, BMW, Audi, Lexus, and Mercedes-Benz continue to set the benchmark, the gap between mainstream and genuine luxury has never been narrower — and one Honda trim is making that argument more convincingly than ever. Honda is rarely the first name that comes up in a luxury SUV conversation, but the top-tier trim of the CR-V Hybrid has changed that calculus. It encroaches meaningfully on what the Mercedes-Benz GLC SUV offers, at a significantly lower price. True to Honda's DNA, this SUV is built for daily use, priced accessibly, and equipped well beyond its segment — and it will make you think twice before writing a much larger check for a Mercedes. This article has been updated to include details and commentary from our test drive of the vehicle. The luxury SUV market in the U.S. has never been bigger or better served. With SUVs dominating the sales charts, it was inevitable that luxury versions would multiply — and nearly every brand now has one. The lines between mainstream and luxury continue to blur. Traditional prestige marques like Ferrari have entered the segment with their first SUV,     the Purosangue BMW continues to rule the roads with models like the X7; Mercedes-AMG has models like the AMG 53, and Lexus is still offering a sensible and restrained lineup. Today's luxury SUVs aren't just nice to sit in; some of them are performance beasts (think the Aston Martin DBX), some of them can off-road as well as old-school mud ruckers (the Lexus GX 550), and some of them pack more tech and comfort features than most homes. The market is exceptionally well catered for, and with prices for some     luxury SUVs below $50,000 there is an option for nearly all budgets. Many would say that Honda doesn't belong in the luxury conversation, sitting a tier below what Mercedes and Cadillac produce. For decades, Honda has earned its reputation by delivering sensible, well-priced, and reliable SUVs that owners can depend on day in and day out. Honda is the parent company of Acura, and while Acura is gaining traction in the SUV market with models like the MDX, ADX, and RDX, Honda itself has rarely attracted high-luxury praise. Take the Honda HR-V as an example: it is well adapted for city and urban driving thanks to its compact footprint, and it can swallow up to 55.1 cubic feet of cargo. The Honda Pilot tells a similar story — it handles off-road duties capably in TrailSport trim, seats seven, and delivers a refined, easy-to-use cabin. Honda, for all its strengths (like     their bulletproof reliability and versatility), isn't exactly the first brand we think of when luxury comes to mind. That perception has shifted with the latest CR-V. The 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid, or a specific trim of it at least, can legitimately be considered a bona fide luxury SUV with the credentials to challenge models from the Mercedes GLC lineup. This compact SUV starts at $30,920, pairs a very fuel-efficient hybrid powertrain with high reliability ratings (83 out of 100 on J.D. Power), and wears a modern yet restrained exterior. On the surface, it sounds very Honda and doesn't scream luxury — but then there is the top-tier trim, the Sport Touring Hybrid. Comparing the base CR-V to the entry-level Mercedes-Benz GLC SUV would be an unfair fight, as the base 2026 GLC 300 already comes equipped with heated front seats, a 12.3-inch digital display, an 11.9-inch touchscreen, wireless phone connectivity, and a 255-horsepower turbo-four. However, the pricing gap between the CR-V and GLC trims is stark and worth examining; the CR-V prices range from $30,920 up to $42,550, while the GLC ranges from $50,900 to $63,500. The Sport Touring Hybrid is where the CR-V's design sharpens into something that feels genuinely upscale. Honda leans into a clean, almost European-inspired aesthetic, with a wide stance, a more assertive front fascia, and a sculpted hood that gives the SUV real road presence. A gloss-black grille, slim LED headlights, and body-color accents mean it looks polished without looking over-styled. The Sport Touring Hybrid also rides on 19-inch machine-finished alloys and features tasteful chrome detailing throughout. Against the GLC, the difference in design philosophy is clear. The GLC leans on brand identity — the prominent star badge, flowing curves, and a sense of occasion baked into every surface. The CR-V counters with a more modern, minimalist approach. Its upright proportions read as practical, while a gently sloping roofline keeps the profile sleek. Around the rear, vertical LED taillights and a subtle roof spoiler give the Sport Touring Hybrid a polished finish, reinforcing the idea that luxury doesn't have to be about badges or long-established heritage. Our team had the opportunity to test drive multiple CR-Vs, among them the Hybrid Sport Touring AWD. We didn't crown it the best because of its performance, in fact, we felt it could use a tad more oomph. We were, however, impressed by how complete the package felt. It's efficient, low-cost ownership make it an ideal choice for anyone looking to stretch their dollar, though it's so much more than simply its money-saving aspects. The cabin is very comfortable, while tech and design are simple yet elegant in their execution. We noted that the CR-V's cabin provides all-day comfort that makes 500+ mile trips pleasant — something very few rivals (luxury or not) can claim. This is thanks to the comfortable, supportive seating and ideal driving position, which are designed to minimize fatigue — and they work! We also took notice of the refined material choices and cabin layout, with our team highlighting the quality that one often expects from vehicles in a much higher price bracket. Material choices are tasteful. Contrasting stitching nicely complements the seats’ supple leather upholstery. What’s more, soft touch materials are placed everywhere your body is likely to touch. The overall effect is one of sophistication, blended carefully with practicality. Simply put, when looking around the Honda’s interior, you won’t be left wondering where the money went. You’ll see it. For many     German SUV fans, it will be a hard sell to accept that a Honda SUV can encroach on Mercedes-Benz levels of luxury — but the top trim of the CR-V makes a compelling case. It is a comfortable, well-appointed, and genuinely refined SUV for considerably less money. We aren't alone in thinking so; while Kelley Blue Book owner scores are moderate at 3.6 out of 5 overall, many owners specifically praise the upscale interior, the driving experience, the exterior design, and the way the suspension absorbs road imperfections. The cabin materials go well beyond what you'd expect from a compact SUV at this price: soft-touch surfaces on the doors and dashboard, a notable absence of cheap-feeling plastics, leather-trimmed seating, and contrast stitching throughout. The interior color palette is muted and sophisticated, with metallic accents and clean lines lending the cabin a refined, almost European character. Armrests and the center console are well padded; the seats are shaped for long journeys with supportive bolstering; dual-zone automatic climate control is standard, and rear-seat air vents are thoughtfully positioned to keep all passengers comfortable. Mechanical refinement comes courtesy of a well-sorted conventional suspension — MacPherson struts up front and a multi-link arrangement at the rear. What stands out is the tuning: Honda has carefully calibrated the dampers and spring rates to absorb bumps with genuine composure while maintaining solid body control. Five drive modes are available (ECON, Normal, Snow, Sport, and Individual), and while there is no adaptive suspension as found on the GLC, the top-tier CR-V delivers a smooth, composed ride that belies its mainstream origins. The technology package in the Sport Touring Hybrid trim helps it punch well above its price point. Honda fits it with a nine-inch touchscreen paired with a fully digital 10.2-inch instrument cluster, creating a cockpit that feels closer to a luxury offering than a mainstream one. Google built-in functionality adds a premium layer of usability, while voice control, app integration, and wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto round out the connected experience. A wireless charging pad, multiple USB ports, and a Bose premium audio system further elevate the interior. On the safety front, the Sport Touring Hybrid comes fully equipped with Honda Sensing, and it is here that the class-encroaching feel becomes most apparent. Features like adaptive cruise control with low-speed follow, lane-keeping assist, collision mitigation braking, and traffic sign recognition combine to deliver a semi-automated driving experience you'd expect from something far more expensive. Add blind-spot monitoring with cross-traffic alert, parking sensors, and a driver-attention monitor, and the top CR-V trim closes the gap between entry-level luxury and the higher-priced German alternatives considerably. The new GLC is without doubt a prestigious SUV, and you do get the Mercedes badge to flaunt instead of the Honda one. You get more power from the engine, and you get the sporty yet dramatic cabin design that has come to define many German marques. However, the top-tier trim of the new CR-V gets a lot of things right where it counts, and makes a case for certain Honda models being viewed as more luxurious than their reputation suggests. This is where the real divide between badge and feel becomes clear. The GLC leans heavily into its identity with bold styling cues, a more aggressive powertrain, and an overall sense of occasion every time you climb in. It feels engineered to remind you that you are driving something premium. The Sport Touring trim takes a different approach, building refinement that isn't immediately obvious but reveals itself through smooth responses, thoughtful ergonomics, and long-term appreciation. The GLC feels like a statement piece, while the CR-V prioritizes ease of use, comfort, and long-term livability. The CR-V doesn't try to mimic the GLC's personality; instead, it closes the gap in the areas that matter most during everyday driving. Strip away the badges, and the margin between the two is narrower than you might expect. This is why the CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid trim makes a compelling alternative to the GLC — and not just on sticker price. The Sport Touring Hybrid is powered by a 2.0-liter inline-four paired with a two-motor hybrid system, mated to a direct-drive transmission and Real Time AWD with Intelligent Control System. The current CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid carries the following specifications. Horsepower and torque are considerably lower than what you get from the 2026 GLC 300, but outright performance is not the CR-V's pitch — its exceptional fuel efficiency is. According to FuelEconomy.gov, the Sport Touring Hybrid achieves 37 combined mpg (40 mpg city, 34 mpg highway), with an estimated annual fuel cost of around $1,600. Fuel isn't the only area where buyers save money. Long-term cost-to-own estimates for the CR-V are substantially lower than those of the GLC. According to CarEdge, the CR-V will cost owners around $7,636 in maintenance and repairs over the first 10 years — below the industry average for mainstream SUVs. The likelihood of the CR-V requiring major repairs sits at 21.74 percent, or 2.85 percent better than average. The GLC's maintenance and repair picture tells a very different story. CarEdge places the German luxury SUV's 10-year maintenance and repair costs at $15,203 — roughly $2,750 more than the industry average for luxury SUVs. The probability of the GLC needing major repairs is also sobering, at 44.09 percent, which is 5.58 percent worse than average. In plain terms, you can expect to spend roughly twice as much maintaining the GLC compared to the CR-V, with a significantly higher risk of serious component failure. Alongside the luxury trimmings and hushed cabin, the CR-V delivers an impressive amount of passenger room and storage. Front legroom measures 41.3 inches; rear legroom is a generous 41 inches; the 60:40 split-folding rear seats open up 76.5 cubic feet of cargo space; and the CR-V can tow up to 1,000 pounds. Despite the spacious interior, it retains city-friendly dimensions. The CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid makes its strongest case in the area that matters most for everyday luxury. It delivers strong efficiency, impressive practicality, and a blend of refinement and usability that feels well beyond what its price suggests. Rather than chasing performance and prestige, Honda has focused on how the top-grade CR-V rides, how quiet the cabin is, how it compares to lower CR-V trims, and the quality of materials throughout. That balance of comfort and efficiency allows it to sit uncomfortably close to far more expensive     luxury German SUVs in perceived quality — even without the badge to match. title: Sample hired as principal in CC/V schools - Colorado Springs Gazette
content:
For Holly Sample, a return to public education after eight years of retirement is another step in a life filled with service to others. Last week, Sample bid farewell to retirement and resumed a career in education, this time as principal of the Cripple Creek-Victor Junior/Senior High School. With 34 years of experience in public education from teaching to administration, Sample is energized by her retirement reversal. In a mode of ready-set-go, Sample begins the year with a list. “My goal is to contribute to the positive school culture that we have and help students learn,” she said. “We are all dedicated to raising students’ levels of learning and connecting with the community.” But first she wants to get kids charged up about school. “I want to make sure that students have great teaching every day in every class,” she said. “I feel confident we’ll be able to do that. We have an amazing staff.” Sample is one of Teller County’s most energetic residents. During her eight-year retirement, she cared for her late mother during five years of illness and volunteered at the Woodland Park Farmers Market and Florissant Fossil Beds National Monument. In the last couple of years, she designed an intern program for the coffee shop at the Aspen Mine Center in Cripple Creek. To get things going, Sample roasted the beans for the shop. Before “retiring,” Sample fulfilled various roles in education, chiefly in Greeley and Fort Collins. In a 34-year career she taught art and special education, developed a business curriculum, served as an assistant principal and helped train teachers in a university school for the University of Northern Colorado. For Sample, accepting the position in Cripple Creek seemed appropriate. “I’m so attached to this community, an amazing community so full of caring people,” she said. “Our school is dedicated to helping students reach their full potential, connecting with families and growing the next community leaders.” In fact, the school faculty reflects Sample’s reverence for community. “My teachers include the mayors of Victor and Cripple Creek, so our leaders are right here working with students,” she said, referring to Barbara Manning, who teaches science, and Annie Durham, who teaches music and drama. Sample had the first week of August to prepare to meet the parents during Back-to-School night Aug. 6, in addition to a pep rally the first day of school Aug. 10. title: The 2027 Ford F-150 Has a New Base Engine and Offers the 5.0-Liter V-8 on More Trims - Car and Driver
content: The twin-turbocharged 2.7-liter V-6 is replaced by the twin-turbo 3.0-liter V-6 that's also found in other Fords such as the Explorer. Ford is gearing up to rejigger the F-150's engine lineup. The incredibly popular pickup truck—which, when combined with the Super Duty, is the bestselling vehicle in the United States—was last refreshed for the 2024 model year, after the truck's 14th generation launched in 2021. It's unclear if the engine changes will be accompanied by styling tweaks as well, but a dealership order guide has now revealed that the F-150 is receiving a new base engine for 2027, along with expanded V-8 availability. See all results for new 2027 Ford F-150 for sale near 82001 The F-150 currently offers a 325-hp twin-turbocharged 2.7-liter V-6 as the entry-level engine, but it appears that is set to change for the 2027 model year. According to the dealership tool, the F-150 will swap out the EcoBoost 2.7-liter V-6 for the EcoBoost 3.0-liter V-6. The 3.0-liter also has twin turbos and is derived from the 2.7-liter V-6. This engine is currently employed by the Ford Explorer; it's standard on the ST and Tremor trims and optional on the Platinum. It can also be found under the hood of the Lincoln Aviator, Ford Ranger Raptor, and Bronco Raptor. In the Explorer, it cranks out 400 horsepower, while it makes 405 ponies in the Ranger Raptor, and 418 hp in the Bronco Raptor. In the Aviator, it produces 383 hp. While we expect the 3.0-liter to out-punch the outgoing 2.7-liter, we're not sure it will quite reach the 400-hp threshold in the F-150, since that would make it step on the toes of the twin-turbocharged 3.5-liter V-6 and the 5.0-liter V-8, both of which produce an even 400 hp and remain available for 2027. The order guide doesn't list horsepower outputs, so we will have to wait to see where this engine lands in the F-150's horsepower hierarchy. Speaking of the V-8, the 5.0-liter will now be available on more trims for 2027. While the King Ranch and Platinum models were previously only available with the 3.5-liter V-6, either in gas-only or hybrid form, the F-150's most luxurious variants will now also offer the V-8, presumably with the same 400-hp output as other F-150s. The EcoBoost 3.5-liter V-6 hybrid powertrain also remains available for the 2027 model year. The order guide shows three new colors for the F-150 in 2027: Birch Sand, Neptune Blue, and Wild Green. Three paint colors from 2026 depart the lineup: Antimatter Blue, Argon Blue, and Avalanche. title: Duke basketball announces Jimmy V Classic matchup against Georgia - The Fayetteville Observer
content: Duke basketball has announced its Dec. 8 matchup against Georgia in the Jimmy V Classic at Madison Square Garden in New York City. College basketball insider Jon Rothstein first reported the matchup May 29 before the Blue Devils officially announced it Tuesday, Aug. 6. The game will be part of a doubleheader that also features Alabama and Houston. The matchup will be the sixth all-time meeting between the Bulldogs and Blue Devils, but the first since 1932. Georgia leads the all-time series 3-2. The Bulldogs are coming off back-to-back NCAA Tournament appearances, while the Blue Devils finished the 2025-26 season 35-3, sweeping the ACC regular-season and tournament titles. The announcement marks Duke's second schedule addition in as many days after the Blue Devils revealed a Dec. 4 home game against Harvard and head coach Tommy Amaker. The Blue Devils' nonconference slate also includes Michigan State, Illinois, Washington State, UConn, Florida, Gonzaga and Texas Tech. Duke will return to Madison Square Garden on Dec. 21 to face the Red Raiders. The Blue Devils will kick things off with a trio of exhibitions against Belmont (Oct. 8), Tennessee (Oct. 20) and Kansas (Oct. 25). Born on June 18, 1942, in Jersey City, New Jersey, he was the son of the late Victor Heidrich and Mary Elizabeth (Fitzmorris) Heidrich. Though “Bud,” as he was known by family and friends, often enjoyed solitude, those who knew him best understood how deeply he valued meaningful relationships. His quiet nature was balanced by a genuine curiosity about others and a love of thoughtful conversation. He never sought recognition or attention, preferring instead to listen, learn, and connect in his own way. During his years as a truck driver, he cherished the opportunity to meet people from all walks of life and formed many lasting friendships along the way. Bud’s curiosity and thirst for knowledge were defining parts of who he was. An avid reader with exceptional vocabulary and a remarkable memory, he possessed a deep understanding of history and countless other subjects. He viewed himself as a steward of history, honoring the stories, craftsmanship, and traditions of the past. As an accomplished marksman and longtime member of the Roslyn Rifle and Revolver Club on Long Island, he valued the memories and friendships he formed. His respect for history was matched by his love of the environment and the natural world. He found peace near the water, especially on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, where he felt most at home. That same appreciation for nature extended to all living creatures. Bud had a special way with animals, and those who knew him smiled at the conversations he carried on with his animal companions as though they were old friends. Music was another lifelong passion. From doo-wop to country, he shared that love with his wife and children through the many concerts they attended together. Bud will be remembered for his quiet humility, intelligence, curiosity, and kindness. Though he often found peace in solitude, he enriched the lives of those around him through his friendships, his love of learning, and his unwavering commitment to preserving the stories and traditions he cherished. Harold is survived by his beloved wife, Lorraine Heidrich; his children, Kenneth Victor Heidrich (Marion) and Kathleen Heidrich; his stepchildren, John Munoz (Erica) and Susan Claire; his grandchildren, Bradford Victor Heidrich (Natalie) and Rita Heidrich; and his step grandchildren, John Munoz and Felicia Gilley. title: Suzuki invests in San Francisco AI fund A.Capital Fund V - International Business Times
content: Suzuki Motor has invested in A.Capital Fund V, a venture fund managed by San Francisco-based A.Capital, through its Silicon Valley corporate venture capital arm Suzuki Global Ventures, the company said on August 6. The fund mainly supports startups in the artificial intelligence sector. Suzuki said the investment is expected to expand Suzuki Global Ventures' access to A.Capital's broader network and help it deepen expertise in AI. Suzuki established Suzuki Global Ventures in October 2022 to work with startups on creating new businesses and business models aimed at delivering value needed by customers and society. The automaker is seeking to accelerate business and technology development by strengthening ties with startups across a range of fields. A.Capital is a venture capital firm based in San Francisco, California. Founded in 2014 by Ronny Conway, it has invested in startups across multiple sectors. Corporate venture capital has become a common route for large manufacturers to gain early exposure to emerging technologies without acquiring startups outright. For automakers, AI is being applied across product development, software, manufacturing and mobility services, making specialist venture funds one way to track innovation trends and potential partners.

title: D.C. v. East Hampton - The East Hampton Star
content: A fight is unfolding over just how far self-governing states and self-governing towns can go in resisting federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement actions in our home communities, with the federal government on one side and New York State and towns like East Hampton on the other. The central question is: Can states or municipalities be compelled to cooperate? Or do we have the right to pass our own laws limiting federal actions that our local population considers unethical, unjust, and un-American? We have been here before. In America, this tension is the tale as old as time. If you weren’t lulled to sleep in history class in seventh grade, you may have a vague recollection of the Fugitive Slave Acts of 1793 and 1850. These were two different laws — escalating in their powers — passed by Congress to enforce the vile and murderous slave-holding system here in America and to compel cooperation from Northern states. The Constitution had since the beginning enshrined the concept that so-called “fugitive slaves” should be returned to their “masters,” but over the years our representatives in Congress, concerned that non-slaveholding states weren’t holding up their end of the bargain enthusiastically enough, felt compelled to pass new, ever harsher legislation to twist the arms of resisters. An accused person had no guaranteed jury trial. Free Black people could legally be kidnapped and carried south. Anyone who obstructed an arrest, helped a fugitive escape, or sheltered one faced fines and imprisonment. In response, Northern states asserted a form of states’ rights against the federal slave regime with so-called “personal liberty laws”: They argued, essentially, that the federal government may enforce its own slave laws, but it could not require our own judges, police, jailers, or public facilities to do the work. In those decades before the Civil War, federal agents entered communities to seize people whom many local residents considered members of those communities. Disputes emerged about due process, mistaken identity, lack of warrants, and access to legal counsel. Shades of 2026. What’s happening this year rings bells of memory, and bells of warning. In January — that dark and terrible month — two American citizens exercising their right to protest were killed by federal ICE agents (Renee Good) and federal Border Patrol agents (Alex Pretti). In May, Gov. Kathy Hochul responded by signing legislation that banned federal agents from hiding their faces, the idea being that law enforcement should not be allowed to operate in anonymity. On Monday, Judge Mae D’Agostino of the Northern District of New York blocked that new law, arguing that New York State cannot restrict the actions of federal officers. It’s state versus Washington, D.C., all over again. Noncooperation laws passed this spring in New York State and East Hampton Town and Village draw an even stronger parallel with 19th-century power struggles between federal and local authority. Our local laws aren’t an attempt to abolish federal immigration rules or to physically prevent ICE from crossing the town line, but they do bar the use of town and village resources to investigate or arrest people for federal civil immigration purposes, absent a judicial warrant. They say exactly what was said in the 1840s: We won’t do the work. Surprise, surprise, this failure to comply has drawn the attention of our representative in Congressman, Nick LaLota. We don’t see a lot of him out east, but he has of late had East Hampton’s name in his mouth more frequently. On Tuesday, he wrote on social media again about our so-called “sanctuary policies” and continues to threaten to withdraw earmarked federal funding from East Hampton if we don’t cooperate. It’s bullying, and it’s obviously grandstanding, intended to win him favor in the White House. He may not have been paying attention in seventh grade, and may not know it yet, but time and the tide of history will prove Mr. LaLota wrong — and prove right those governments (of whatever size) that resist unjust and un-American actions by federal agents. title: Hennessey Blackbird is an All-V-8, Manual-only Hypercar - The ClassicCars.com Journal
content: Stats and performance figures are important parts of performance vehicles, but they’re not everything. Sure, a turbocharged hybrid engine connected to a dual-clutch automatic and all-wheel drive — an increasingly common formula — can make a car fast as hell, but all those components make it more complex and put so much tech between the driver and the fundamentals of the machine. The upcoming Hennessey Blackbird strips all that away, leaving a naturally aspirated V-8, six-speed manual gearbox, and rear-wheel drive. For 35 years, the name Hennessey has been synonymous with more power and greater capabilities. The Hennessey Performance division has turned out everything from twin-turbo Dodge Vipers to 1,000-horsepower Ford F-150 Raptor-based VelociRaptoR 1000s. Within the last decade, Hennessey Special Vehicles (HSV) has made its own hypercars, starting with the Venom F5, a swoopy road rocket with a 1,817-horsepower twin-turbo V8, F1-inspired steering yoke, and paddle shifters. The more focused Venom F5 Revolution has a top speed of more than 250 mph and set a production car lap record at the Circuit of the Americas with a time of 2:10.90. As its name implies, the Blackbird was inspired by the Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird aircraft, which set a speed record by flying from Los Angeles to Washington, D.C., in 1 hour, 4 minutes, and 20 seconds, so it’s going to be fast, but it’s about more than that. Company founder and CEO John Hennessey said, “From the beginning, Blackbird was guided by a simple idea: to deliver an analog experience where beauty and drama define every moment. This is not a numbers car.” In fact, the Blackbird is meant to be a touring car that someone can drive more than 800 miles in a day. To make it more long-distance-friendly, HSV gave it a larger greenhouse and a cabin with more passenger and storage space than the Venom F5, as well as an adaptive suspension, ABS, traction control, four cup holders, and enough room in the front trunk for two full-size carry-on bags. Of course, the Blackbird will be able to fly across those long distances — even it doesn’t make the trip in record time. It’s based on an all-new bespoke carbon fiber tub, which is covered in carbon fiber body work, all of which should weigh less than 3,000 pounds. Aviation and motorsports filtered into the overall design. The noticeable “chine line” crease in the doors and the rear vertical stabilizers, which deploy at 71 mph and stand at +/- 71 degrees, are undeniably SR-71. Formula One influenced the look of the side pods; LMP1 Le Mans race cars inspired the winglets. The diamond-shaped arrangement for the quad exhaust outlets was taken from a different aircraft: the Bell X-1, which became the first airplane to fly faster than the speed of sound in 1947. Working with Ilmor Engineering, Hennessey developed the Blackbird’s propulsion system: a naturally aspirated 6.2-liter V-8 with a target output of 800-850 horsepower and the ability to rev to more than 9,000 rpm. If the six-speed manual is shifted perfectly, the Blackbird should be able to reach 60 mph in only 2.5 seconds — an impressive time for a three-pedal car channeling that kind of firepower through just the rear Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 tires. Flat out, the Blackbird has a projected top speed of 220 mph. The gullwing doors open to a cabin that’s fittingly simplified and focused. Behind the flat-bottom wheel is a centrally mounted tachometer. There are no screens, although a special holster keeps the driver’s phone in place to run Apple CarPlay or Android Auto. The center bridge houses the exposed linkage and gated shifter for the six-speed gearbox. Of course, there are aviation-themed elements, such as the structure on top of the dashboard that resembles the SR-71 and its afterburner plumes, and the dash-mounted “whiskey compass.” Hennessey won’t start producing the Blackbird until 2029-2030, but more than two-thirds of the 71-unit production run have been claimed already, each priced from $2.5 million (before taxes). Whether you’re just curious about the Blackbird or impatiently awaiting the production/delivery of your very own, you can see the Texas-based automaker’s newest model in-person at The Quail, A Motorsports Gathering on Friday, August 14. title: Above and Below — Jesse V. Johnson [Review] - In Review Online
content: As InRO‘s own Jake Tropila makes note of in his recent piece on the killer-shark-in-a-cave-movie The Devil’s Mouth, “shark movies have been seemingly omnipresent all year”; he goes on to cite Deep Water, Thrash, The Bay, and Chum as but the most recent examples. Into this crowded field we can also welcome Jesse V. Johnson’s Above and Below, which adds gangsters to an already deadly stew. Johnson is, of course, one of our finest contemporary action specialists, one of the masters of the American DTV scene. And while he’s likely best known for high-powered hand-to-hand combat (often starring martial artist Scott Adkins), Johnson has also dipped his toes into medieval combat (Boudica), a Sam Fuller-inspired war thriller (Hell Hath No Fury), and the neo-Western (last year’s Thieves Highway). Above and Below is his first excursion into creature feature territory, but Johnson brings his typical steady hand and no-nonsense practicality to a genre often rife with absurdities and implausibilities. While the majority of the films mentioned above contrive ludicrous scenarios to put humans in the way of prehistoric death machines, Johnson’s humble film takes the shape of a small-scale, high-stakes thriller where sharks are just one of several obstacles. It takes a few minutes to introduce all the players who will set the plot in motion: Tatiana (Laura Marano), her best friend Kayle (Christina Ochoa), and their respective boyfriends are partying in Mexico. It’s a last hurrah of sorts, as they’ll all soon be going their separate ways once they return to the States. While the core group drinks and dances at a club, Tatiana’s brother Kyle (Diego Llinas) is in the midst of a poker game with high roller Burns (Antonio Banderas). Kyle thinks he’s got a winning hand and goes all in, only to be stymied by the charming but shifty Burns. As a conciliatory gesture, Burns offers Kyle and his friends a tour on a shark sightseeing boat, free of charge. While Kyle doesn’t tell anyone about losing his entire life savings, he does tell them about the tour. Everyone loves the idea, and the next day they’re boarding a sleek, modern yacht, eager to drink and see some sharks (from the safety of a protective cage, of course). Tensions quickly mount, however, when a couple of shady-looking guys also climb aboard, several duffle bags in tow. Kyle protests, saying that Burns guaranteed them a private tour experience, but the captain obviously knows these men and is powerless to turn them away. Martin (DTV mainstay Louis Mandylor) and Garrison (French MMA fighter Jess Liaudin) make themselves comfortable, as the boys go down under the water first and the girls sunbathe on the boat deck. Eventually, it’s the girls’ turn in the cage, but while they plunge into the murky depths, one of the boys accidentally opens a duffle bag. To their surprise, there’s a bunch of drugs in it, and Martin immediately shoots some people. Soon, Burns and another henchman have been called to the scene, revealing Banderas as the local kingpin and Martin and Garrison as two of his bagmen. There are suddenly some dead bodies lying around, two young women trapped underwater with limited oxygen, and a bag filled to the brim with kilos of drugs tossed overboard, floating in shark-infested waters. Plenty more twists and turns are in store, and it would be remiss to spoil their pleasures or practicalities here. Suffice to say, Johnson maintains a clean, simple style as these various events unfold, as each character attempts to solve an immediate problem at hand only to find another immediately popping up. Above and Below‘s locations are limited to the boat deck and the shark cage tethered beneath it, and the film’s low budget precludes big CGI set pieces or huge, explosive action scenes. But there are ample delights to be found in watching people problem-solve, as the characters navigate their various predicaments. Johnson is a fine craftsman, and his bits-and-bolts approach emphasizes precision and visual clarity. It’s always clear where characters are in proximity to each other, with only the occasional shark or cartel gunman popping into the frame to wreak havoc. Johnson pulls from Spielberg by hiding the sharks as much as possible, filming them in quick little peeks — a fin here, a close-up of gaping jaws there. Mandylor, meanwhile, is having an absolute hoot, bringing an unhinged, wildcard energy to the proceedings, and Banderas is aces as a suave, unfailingly polite drug lord ( the kind of guy who will give a genuinely heartfelt apology before dispatching with someone nonetheless). Above and Below is undoubtedly a modest picture — there’s that word again — but one that knows its job and does it with aplomb. The DTV faithful will be pleased, and hopefully any others lucky enough to catch up with this summer cinema pleasure. DIRECTOR: Jesse V. "The timing of performance is determined according to the local time at the place where the payment obligation is to be performed." The decision clarifies how payment deadlines should be assessed where banking days are defined by reference to multiple jurisdictions. Songa confirms that, absent clear wording to the contrary, the timing of performance is determined according to the local time at the place where the payment obligation is to be performed. Under the memorandum of agreement (“MOA”), the sellers agreed to sell MT “Songa Coral” to the buyers for US$25m. Banking Days was defined in the MOA as the days banks were open in certain listed locations: “‘Banking Days’ are days on which banks are open both in the country of the currency stipulated for the Purchase Price in Clause 1 (Purchase Price) and in the place of closing stipulated in Clause 8 (Documentation) and United States of America, Canada, United Kingdom, Switzerland, Turkey, UEA [sic], Greece, Norway (add additional jurisdictions as appropriate).” (para 6) The various jurisdictions spread across different time zones and the parties disagreed as to when the final Banking Day expired in relation to a dispute as to whether the purchase price had been paid on time. The following events took place, leading to the dispute before the Commercial Court: The key issue for the tribunal was whether the buyers breached the MOA by failing to provide the agreed purchase money by midnight Norwegian time on 8 September 2022. The arbitrators sided with the buyers’ arguments. In their partial final award, the arbitrators held that the notice of termination was served too early and that the buyers could only have been in breach if the funds had not been paid by midnight on 8 September 2022 in Hawaii (the most westerly jurisdiction listed in the definition of Banking Days). The tribunal held that the definition of Banking Days was determinative as to the start and end of a day. It therefore held that the time for performance under clause 3 expired at midnight at the end of 8 September 2022 in Hawaii. Applying principles of ordinary contractual construction, the tribunal was “unable to see how the words used, when reading the definition of ‘Banking Days’ into clause 3, could properly be said to give rise to any other meaning” (para 15). Although the tribunal recognised that this displaced the prima facie presumption that an obligation to be performed in a particular place must be performed by midnight there, it took the view that the express language in the definition displaced that usual presumption. "The tribunal held that the definition of Banking Days was determinative as to the start and end of a day." The sellers appealed on a point of law under section 69 of the Arbitration Act 1996. They argued before the High Court that the MOA’s definition of “Banking Days” identified which calendar days qualified as Banking Days but did not define when a day began or ended. The sellers’ appeal was allowed. The court held that the sellers’ notice to cancel was valid. The court assessed what the definition as applied in clause 3 would convey to the reasonable person: “The definition of “Banking Days” does not purport to tell one what is meant by “day”, nor broaden that word’s ordinary meaning, nor fix its start or its end. It takes all that for granted… The “definition” of “Banking Days” does not tell us what a day is, or when it starts or finishes. It simply tells us which calendar days… count as Banking Days: that some calendar days are Banking Days, and other calendar days are not.” (para 24) In reaching his conclusion, the judge considered several factors and took the view that “Banking Days” in the MOA referred to calendar days. He held that the tribunal had erred in treating the definition of “Banking Days” as determining the start and end of a day and that decision was incorrect in law. Once 8 September 2022 had been identified as the relevant day, the question was whether payment was made before midnight local time at the place of performance, Norway. The judge explained that a broad reading of the definition would risk producing a “day” which lasts for 37 or 38 hours (depending on the time of the year), starting at midnight in the UAE and ending at midnight in Hawaii. He considered it unlikely that the parties intended to create a “day” in which the various jurisdictions noted in the definition would pass through three different calendar dates, potentially creating significant contractual uncertainty. Further, in the judge’s view, the MOA used relative and not absolute terms – it did not define a fixed calendar date, but one that was calculated by reference to an interval. Ultimately, the judge explained that the logical place to look to in identifying where a day began and ended was where the act in question has been or is to be performed (following the leading authority of Euronav NV v Repsol Trading SA (The Maria) [2022] 1 Lloyd’s Rep 247). In this case the obligation to release the balance of the purchase price was to be performed in Norway. Songa provides the following helpful practical takeaways: "A broad reading of the definition would risk producing a “day” which lasts for 37 or 38 hours." title: 700-V GaN Semiconductors Enhance Energy Efficiency in High-Demand Apps - Electronic Design
content: The independent technology information source for electronics developers The 700-V PowerGaN devices in STMicroelectronics’ STPOWER portfolio of gallium-nitride (GaN)-based semiconductors are designed to improve efficiency and increase power density in high-demand applications such as artificial intelligence (AI). Like all members of the PowerGaN family, they offer low conduction losses, very low switching loss at high operating frequencies, and zero reverse-recovery charge, leading to reduced system size, weight, and operating temperature. Engineered for a 700-V rating, they support reliable high-power operation and higher-frequency power-conversion topologies in AI, robotics, industrial power supplies, and smart-grid converters for energy generation, distribution, and storage. The seven new GaN enhancement-mode transistors (HEMTs) now joining the PowerGaN series cover a wide range of continuous current ratings, from 6 to 29 A, and typical RDS(on) is from 53 to 270 mΩ. The devices share the ultra-low internal capacitances and low gate charge, inherent in GaN wide-bandgap technology, giving them a QG × RDS(on) figure of merit (FOM) significantly ahead of traditional silicon devices. Qualified to ST’s stringent reliability standards, the devices can drop into power‑conversion circuits as a replacement for MOSFETs, or enable new, higher‑frequency topologies. Their capability to operate at elevated switching frequencies reduces the size of magnetics and passives, enabling a more compact power stage and higher power density. The DPAK, TOLL, and PowerFLAT surface-mount packages are proven in practice and widely supported by major electronic design automation libraries and toolchains. The TOLL and PowerFLAT devices provide a Kelvin source connection that separates the gate-control circuit from the main power path to maximize noise immunity, protect the gate driver, and preserve timing margin. The new transistors are in production now and priced at $0.63 to $2.25 for orders of 1,000 pieces. Lee is the author of the popular PowerBites series. The inaugural Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series is finally here with the All Blacks embarking on their first tour of South Africa in 30 years. As is tradition, the men from New Zealand kick off their tour against a local team, with the Stormers first on Dave Rennie’s charges’ hit list. This will be the first-ever meeting between the Stormers and All Blacks in what promises to be an epic night at the DHL Stadium in Cape Town. New Zealand arrive on African soil with a new head coach who has been tasked with getting their Rugby World Cup bid back on track, and so far, the former Wallabies boss has delivered with the All Blacks going three from three in July. They defeated France, Italy and Ireland, respectively, during the Nations Championship, and whilst the Springboks will be the main challenge for Rennie and his charges in South Africa, they will be wary not to slip up against the United Rugby Championship teams, with the Stormers being one of their biggest threats. Despite being without nine Springboks stars, John Dobson has still managed to name a strong matchday 23 for the historic fixture. Many regular starters from last season feature with a healthy mix of experience, youth and X-factor littered throughout. That means that Rennie’s men won’t get an easy ride in the Mother City, and that’s precisely what they would be hoping for. The matches against the URC teams are not just an opportunity to get match minutes in preparation for the Boks, but they can provide answers for the coaches on tactics and player selections. It also allows fringe players the opportunity to force their way up the pecking order for the Test matches, and the harder the opposition, the better for the All Blacks. While Rennie’s men will be the favourites heading into the match, they will know that they will be sternly challenged in multiple facets of the game, particularly up front. The Stormers have a reputation for being an attractive attacking team, but the foundation of their game is one not too dissimilar from the Springboks, with power and set-piece accuracy being paramount. The URC semi-finalists produced a 91% lineout success rate in the competition, a percentage only bettered by champions Leinster (92%), while they also won more scrum penalties (64) than any other club. Sure, they will be without the services of Zachary Porthen, which is a blow, but in Neethling Fouché, Vernon Matongo, Ntuthuko Mchunu, and Sazi Sandi, they have brutally effective scrummaging props. “Parity up front is important, or dominance to be fair. It’s going to be a physical game; set-piece is very important,” Beauden Barrett told reporters, and he is right. The All Blacks have identified the threat; the question is, can they do anything about it? The scrum is a massive weapon for the Stormers, and if they have any hope of clinching a historic result, they will need reward from it. Barrett is an experienced campaigner and has played against South African clubs many a time before, and his verdict that the All Blacks will need parity up front extends beyond the set-pieces and rightly so. The Stormers had an astute defence last season and have the ball-carrying threats to really trouble the All Blacks. Being able to stop the men in blue and white hoops before they get momentum will be key, with Evan Roos being the main threat in the forward pack. All Blacks: Dave Rennie dealt blow for Stormers clash as star forward denied chance to push for Test recall The topic of South African teams leaving Super Rugby was understandably raised again this week with Rennie weighing in. “I still think it’s a real pity South Africa aren’t part of Super Rugby,” he said after naming his team. “It was pretty special, and I understand why. “It’s a hell of a lot easier. They’ll go north, fly overnight, wake up there, same time zone. But it was a pretty special part of Super Rugby to come over here and challenge yourself against great sides in tough conditions.” The head coach has handed veteran playmaker Barrett his first start of the year after he missed the opening three Tests. The 35-year-old is raring for the challenge but is wary not to get ahead of himself. “I know how excited I am and I’m conscious that I don’t want to overdo it either, like overplay,” he said. “It’s about containing that and making good decisions because there has been a few weeks between games for me. So there might be a tendency to really rip in and get stuck in, but at the same time it’s about controlling those emotions, those temptations, and just backing myself in the preparation.” Fellow veteran, Deon Fourie, will mark his comeback from injury against the All Blacks. The soon-to-be 40-year-old has endured a truly torrid run of injuries over the past two years but has the opportunity to tackle the men from Aotearoa again after his heroic efforts in the Rugby World Cup final in 2023. “I am definitely raring to go, and it’s a great opportunity. I was looking forward to this match since it was announced a year or two ago,” he said earlier in the week. “Just to represent your club, where I’ve spent almost my entire career, against a Test side like the All Blacks is such a big occasion. To face the Haka is something every little boy dreams of when they start playing rugby.” Rassie Erasmus ‘not scared to say’ Greatest Rivalry should have been earlier as Springboks boss issues ‘burnout’ warning Three years ago, Deon Fourie produced arguably the performance of his career – he has an incredible catalogue of top-drawer shifts – when he came off the bench for Bongi Mbonambi in the Rugby World Cup final. The relentless forward makes a timely return from injury to be named on the side of the scrum for the showdown with New Zealand and is bound to wreak havoc. A breakdown master, Fourie is a real workhorse around the park as he proved in that final and remains a seriously strong and athletic ball carrier despite being 39 years old. New Zealanders might know Stormers captain Ruhan Nel better for his brilliance on the sevens scene, but since making the switch to the 15-aside game, he has become a classy outside centre, a glue-man for the Cape-based team’s backline and leader of the defence. Nel is one of the more experienced campaigners in the squad and will be crucial in leading the defence in particular. With the set-pieces being crucial in this fixture, the performance of Andre-Hugo Venter will be under the spotlight. The 24-year-old was released by Rassie Erasmus to represent the Stormers in this game, which also serves as an opportunity for him to prove that he can mix it with a top international team after earning his two caps against Portugal and Wales. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Similarly, the clash is a massive opportunity for All Blacks hookers Samisoni Taukei’aho and Asafo Aumua. Codie Taylor misses the match through injury and is primed for a return ahead of the first Test. It’s plainly obvious that Taylor is Rennie’s first-choice in the number two jersey, but the next in line is less clear with Taukei’aho and Aumua battling it out for the 16 shirt. A big shift against a powerful Stormers pack could go a long way for either man to claim that jersey. It’s also a huge chance for Rieko Ioane to stamp his mark after being overlooked for the Nations Championship matches. The 29-year-old had a turbulent spell at Leinster, where he struggled to really shine. Ioane fell out of favour with Scott Robertson last year and that hasn’t changed with Rennie taking over. Once a regular starter in the number 13 shirt, Ioane has been named on the wing to face the Stormers – perhaps the position where he has a better chance of getting regular game time. Rennie’s team is littered with players who have a point to prove and have been given the chance to force their way into the Test team. Ethan Blackadder certainly fits into that category with the Crusaders star earning his first appearance in the black jersey since starting at Ellis Park back in 2024. The 31-year-old was in incredible form at the time but has had a troublesome run of injuries since. He enjoyed a strong run of form during the latter stages of the Super Rugby Pacific season and could be a real weapon for Rennie in the back-row. All Blacks team: Five takeaways as Beauden Barrett entering ‘last chance saloon territory’ following Dave Rennie’s ‘fascinating’ selection When a player of Beauden Barrett’s experience and calibre dubs a player ‘the future’, one cannot help but keep an eye on him, and that’s precisely what he said of his opposing number 10, Yaqeen Ahmed. The duo are at completely different points of their careers, with Barrett being the master of the trade, a two-time World Rugby Player of the Year, a World Cup winner and an all-time great of the All Blacks. At 35 years old, he is on the decline as he isn’t as rapid as he once was, but he still operates at an elite level with his tactical kicking and overall game management. The master will look to flex his outrageous skill-set in Cape Town once again and outfox the Stormers apprentice. Ahmed makes his Stormers debut against the All Blacks, with the 20-year-old handed the reins after starring for the Junior Boks, the side who defended their World Rugby Junior World Championship. We saw during that tournament just how talented the Wynberg Boys’ High School old boy is. He has all the tricks in the toolbox to be really successful at the highest level. A raw talent, he is a triple-threat – run, kick and pass – fly-half, but also had a real swagger and attitude about him, something that is needed in the position. We saw the rawness, though, against Zimbabwe when he was red-carded, and what will be crucial is the ability to remain cool and collected when facing the All Blacks. While the battle up front is bound to decide the fixture, there is no more box-office head-to-head than the one in the number 10 jumpers. Beauden Barrett ‘honoured’ to be Stormers’ Junior Bok star’s inspiration: ‘He’s certainly the future’ The All Blacks are comfortable favourites heading into what could be a real banana skin match for Rennie, who has made a plethora of changes for the tour opener. It’s also arguably the club that has the best chance of knocking over the tourists. Dobson’s charges are bound to wreak havoc over the 80 minutes, and suggestions that the All Blacks will rack up a cricket score are well off the mark. The Stormers will be physical, aggressive and highly motivated to clinch a historic result and have the talent to do it. They have a front-row and scrum capable of winning penalties, power carriers that can get them on the front foot and backs like Ahmed, Imad Khan and Warrick Gelant who can create something out of nothing. The All Blacks have the players who ticked all of those boxes too, and the major difference is they just have more of them. We can certainly expect a tight first half where the Stormers stay in the fight and go toe-to-toe with the All Blacks but Rennie’s men are bound to pull away in the final quarter in particular. In the historic first-ever meeting between these two proud teams, we predict that the All Blacks will surge to a comfortable 20-point victory.
